senses.gloss:
Kāmakalā
------------------------------------------
A tāntrik ideology, कामकला represents the Divine मोथेर् (Tripurasundarī) in terms of three bindus or dots, arranged in a triangular form. The dot at the apex is said to be the face and the other two dots, the breasts.
The three dots separately indicate the three powers—kriyāśakti, इच्छाशक्ति and ज्ञानशक्ति (powers of action, will and knowledge)—and their presiding deities ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव.
The conception is esoteric and mystical.

kamaṇḍalu
(‘that which brings the essence of water’)
------------------------------------------
A saṁnyāsin (Hindu monk) who has renounced all possessions is permitted to keep and use a few things absolutely essential for living. One of them is the कमण्डलु or the water pot, usually made of bitter gourd (and sometimes of clay). It has a handle, a lid and a spout. He is expected to carry it, along with the पवित्र (cloth for straining water).

Kāmaśāstra
(‘treatise dealing with love’)
------------------------------------------
In the Hindu scheme of life embodied in the धर्मशास्त्रस्, काम or sexual love also has been given a place, as the third puruṣārtha, end to be striven for in life. Hence, like many other fields of knowledge कामशास्त्र or erotics too has been developed as a science.
Erotic elements are not rare even in the वेदस्. The Vedic seers appear to have had a realistic approach to the process of procreation.
Quite a few sages like श्वेतकेतु, बाभ्रव्य, दत्तक, Cārāyaṇa and Kucumāra have been cited as authorities on the कामशास्त्र.
Vātsyāyana’s Kāmasūtras—Vātsyā-yana (3rd century A. D.) was also known as Mallanāga—seems to be the earliest and basic work on erotics. Yaśodhara’s (13th century A. D.) Jayamaṅgalā is the standard commentary on the same.
Other works cited on this science of erotics are: Nāgarasarvasva (of Padmaśrī, 10th century A. D.), Ratirahasya (of Kokkoka), Anaṅgaraṅga (of Kalyāṇamalla-deva), Kandarpacūḍāmaṇi (of वीरभद्र, A. D. 1577) and so on.
The Vājīkaraṇa section of the आयुर्वेद is related to the science of erotics.
Some Western scholars like Pisanus Fraxi have admired the decency and finesse with which the subject of erotics has been handled by the Indian writers, who were interested in preventing disharmony between the husband and the wife and not in promoting sensual indulgence.

Kāmeśvarī
(‘goddess lording over desires,’ ‘granter of desires’)
------------------------------------------
She is the counterpart of शिव as कामेश्वर. (See KĀMEŚVARA.) She is an aspect of कामाख्या. (See KĀMĀKHYĀ.)
Iconographical works describe her as dark in complexion. She has six faces, eighteen eyes and twelve arms. She carries पुस्तक (book), siddhasūtra (thread), पञ्चबाण (five arrows), खड्ग (sword), शक्ति and śūla (spears), अक्षमाला (rosary), पद्म (lotus), kodaṇḍa (bow), abhaya मुद्रा (gesture of protection), carma (shield), and पिनाक (spear-bow), in her arms.
Her six faces are of different colours and represent six deities: white (Māheś-varī), red (Kāmākhyā), yellow (Tripurā), green (Śāradā), black (Kāmeśvarī) and variegated (Candrā).
Multicoloured garments and tiger skin adorn her.
Worship of कामेश्वरी is done in the श्रीचक्र. (See ŚRĪCAKRA.)

Kāmandaka
------------------------------------------
The Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य or चाणक्य (300 B. C.) was a monumental work on political science and allied fields of knowledge. However, its language being rather terse and prosaic, कामन्दक (or Kāmandaki) rendered its contents into more elegant poetry, elucidating the teachings and adding didactic tales. This work is known as Nītisāra or Kāmandakīya Nītisāra.
Kāmandaka might have lived any where during the period A. D. 300 to A. D. 600.
The work Nītisāra is in 20 cantos and 36 prakaraṇas. The contents may be briefly summarised as follows:
Cantos 1 to 3:Discipline and training of the king and the princes. Varṇāśrama धर्म. General rules of conduct. Cantos 4 to 7:The Saptāṅgas or the seven elements of the State. Cantos 8 to 12:Inter-state relationships, treatises, nature of hostilities and diplomatic counter-moves. Canto 13:Envoys, ambassadors and spies. Canto 14:Glorious results of strenuous actions and initiatives taken on time. Canto 15:Vices and their consequent afflictions. Canto 16:Enemy aggression and measures to combat it. Cantos 17 to 19:Army movements and political expedients. Assessment of one’s strength and rectifying one’s weaknesses. Canto 20:Deployment of the armed forces in offensive and defensive warfare. Kāmandaka openly acknowledges his indebtedness to कौटिल्य.
The significant omissions in कामन्दक’s work are: internal administration, theories of taxation and regulation of trade and commerce.
The work has Balinese and Jāvanese versions.
See also ARTHAŚĀSTRA.

Kāmākṣī
------------------------------------------
Kāñcīpuram (the modern town Kanchi or Conjeevaram in Tamil Nadu) is one of the seven very ancient sacred cities described in the Hindu scriptures.
The goddess in the देवी temple attached to the Ekāmranātha temple complex is known as कामाक्षी, ‘one with beautiful eyes’.
It is said that once when शिव and गौरी quarelled during a game of dice, शिव cursed गौरी to become ugly. With विष्णु’s grace she obtained lovely features with beautiful eyes. Then by performing severe austerities under a single mango tree (= eka + āmra), she pleased शिव and was reunited with him.
This goddess has several names: Kāmakoṭṭam, Devagarbhā, Kāmakaṇṇi and कामेश्वरी.
Kāmākṣī is shown as seated in the पद्मासन with four hands. In the upper right and left hands she is holding the aṅkuśa (goad) and पाश (noose). The other two hands are holding lotuses. A parrot is also shown at the back.
There is a श्रीचक्र or a Śrīyantra, established by शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820), in front of the image, on the ground. Worship is offered to this यन्त्र.
The story goes that originally this goddess was fierce and used to come out of the temple at dead of night to devour the people who had incurred her wrath. When शङ्कर came to know of it, he appeased her and exhorted a promise that she would not stir out of the temple without his permission!
The tradition of taking शङ्कर’s permission (whose image also has been established in the temple complex) before the उत्सवमूर्ति or the procession image is moved out, is kept up even now.
See also KĀÑCĪPURAM.

Kāmārpukūr
------------------------------------------
In हिन्दुइस्म्, a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे is called tīrthakṣetra. The word tīrtha refers to any place considered sacred due to its association with a holy river, a mountain, a temple or any other object. More often, it may be due to its close connection with a great spiritual or reli-gious leader. And, the two remote villages of Bengal—Kāmārpukūr and Jayarāma-bāṭī, the birth places of Śrī रामकृष्ण and Sāradādevī—have become famous tīrthakṣetras or places of पिल्ग्रिमगे exactly due to this reason.
The town of कामार्पुकूर् is 112 kms. (70 miles) to the north-west of Calcutta (now, Kolkata). The ancestral होउसे where Śrī Rāmakṛṣṇa—better known as the Paramahaṁsa—was born was taken over by the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् and the Rama-krishna Mission and a beautiful temple raised over his birthplace.
The main shrine which is the birth place, contains an elegant marble image of Śrī रामकृष्ण.
The small temple of Raghuvīr (Rāma), the family deity of Śrī रामकृष्ण’s ancestors, the room where Śrī रामकृष्ण used to live and associated structures have been maintained in a good condition.
Other places connected with his boyhood days like the small temple of शिव (where his मोथेर् had a unique mystical experience), the village tank Haldārpukūr, the village school—which is a shed—and the houses of the Lahā family are also there to be visited.
The following are the major religious festivals celebrated at this centre: birthdays of Śrī रामकृष्ण, Sāradādevī and Vivekānanda; दुर्गापूजा; Mahāśivarātrī and Kālīpūjā.
The centre is running schools, hostels and a dispensary apart from conducting several rural welfare activities. There are good facilities for the pilgrim-devotees who throng the place throughout the year.

Kāmākhyā
(‘[Goddess] known as [the fulfiller of] desires’)
------------------------------------------
Worship of God as देवी or शक्ति, the Divine मोथेर्, is as old as the वेदस्. Most of the aspects and forms of the देवी are those of पार्वती. In the पुराणस्, legends connected with पार्वती and her spouse, Lord शिव, are legion. One of these is the story of the destruction of the sacrifice of दक्ष by शिव whose spouse सती had immolated herself in the sacrificial ground, unable to bear the insult to her husband.
कामाख्या">The Temple of KāmākhyāWhen शिव was carrying the dead body of सती on his back and roaming about the world with inconsolable grief, ब्रह्मा and विष्णु cleverly managed to enter into that body and cut it into 51 pieces. Every place, where a piece of that body fell, became a sacred spot and came to be known as a Śaktipīṭha, the seat of शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर्. कामाख्या is one such Śaktipīṭha where the yoni (generative organ) is said to have fallen.
The temple of कामाख्या is situated on a hill known as ‘Nīlācala’ 5 kms. (3 miles) from Guwahati, the capital city of Assam. There is also a small township here. The district itself is known as Kamrup (Kāmarūpa).
This region of Assam was earlier known as ‘Prāgjyotiṣapura,’ ruled by the king नरक, who was killed by Śrī कृष्ण. It got the new name ‘Kāmarūpa’ after काम (cupid) was restored to life by शिव here and a temple for the देवी was built by विश्वकर्म, the architect of gods.
The present temple has been built by the king नर-नारायण of Coochbihar in A. D. 1565, after the earlier one had been destroyed by the Muslim iconoclast Kalapahar.
The architecture of the temple is simple. The शिखर (dome over the sanctum) follows the beehive pattern. Parts of the older temple are also seen in the lower portion.
The temple houses no image of the goddess. There is a cave within the temple in a corner of which stands a block of stone with the symbol of a yoni sculptured on it. It is kept moist from the oozings of a natural spring within the cave. The devotees touch it and offer flowers and leaves.
Among the sculptures adorning the temple structure may be mentioned dancing गणेश and चामुण्डा. The former is charming whereas the latter is fierce.
Other temples on the Nīlācala are those of घण्टाकर्ण, तारा, भैरवी and भुवनेश्वरी.
The most important festivals celeb-rated at this temple are अम्बुवाची, Debaddhani and दुर्गापूजा. (See AMBUVĀCĪ and DURGĀPŪJĀ.) The second festival is connected with the goddess मनसा (snake-goddess, identified with जरत्कारु, daughter of the serpent king वासुकि).
Animal sacrifice during the festivals exists even today.
When shown as an icon, कामाख्या is pictured or sculptured as a youthful lady, yellowish-red in colour with unbraided hair, having three eyes and two hands (showing the abhaya and varada mudrās). She is seated on a red lotus. The sun and the मोओन् are her ear-ornaments.

kāma
(‘desire’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most widely used words in the religio-philosophical as also mythological literature, ‘kāma’ has three meanings: a) desire in general; b) cupid, the god of lust and c) lust.
Kāma, also known as मन्मथ, Madana, Kandarpa and Anaṅga, was the son of ब्रह्मा. When ब्रह्मा gave him the boon of the power to delude the whole world with lust, he dared to use it against ब्रह्मा himself! Then ब्रह्मा cursed him to be reduced to ashes by the third eye of Lord शिव. At the earnest entreaties of रति, his wife, शिव revived him.
Iconographical works depict him as a handsome young man with a bow of sugarcane and five arrows tipped with flowers. He is accompanied by his two wives, रति and Tṛṣā and rides on a parrot. His banner is a मकर or crocodile.
Kāma as desire in general, can be good or bad. A good desire, as the desire for मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्, elevates whereas bad desires prove to be formidable obstacles in the path of spiritual evolution.
Kāma as lust, has been considered as one of the four पुरुषार्थस् or ends to be striven for, in life. Since procreation was considered as one of the sacred duties of duly married couples, काम has been given that status. However, it has always to be within the limits set by धर्म or righteousness as described in the scriptures. Transgressions have been severely condemned and punishments also prescribed.
See also PURUṢĀRTHAS.

Kāmbhoja
------------------------------------------
One of the countries (and its people) well-known in the ancient days, काम्भोज was the region to the north-west of India, extending from the Punjab to Bactria or Balkh. It was probably to the north of the present day Kabul.
The country was known for its excellent breed of horses and great warriors. It was considered as a ‘Mahājanapada’ or ‘a great country’.
Sudakṣiṇa was the king ruling over it during the days of the महाभारत. He sided with the Kauravas and was killed by अर्जुन in the कुरुक्षेत्र war.

kāmyeṣṭi
(‘desire-motivated sacrifice’)
------------------------------------------
Since all our desires cannot be fulfilled by human resources and efforts alone, the Vedic sages provided in the system of sacrifices some special ones for this purpose. They are generally called kāmyeṣṭis (kāmya = desired object; इष्टि = sacrifice).
A very short list of such sacrifices is given here as a sample:
Annakāmeṣṭi for plenty of ड़ोओद्.
Ayuṣkāmeṣṭi for long life.
Darśapūrṇamāsa for attaining हेअवेन्.
Kārīrīṣṭi for getting rains.
Pavamāneṣṭi for the cure of chronic diseases.
Putrakāmeṣṭi for begetting worthy sons.
Vasukāmeṣṭi for attaining wealth.
These are performed on the new-मोओन् or full-मोओन् days and are variants of the Darśa sacrifice.
See also VEDIC SACRIFICES.

Kāmeśvara
(‘lord of desires’)
------------------------------------------
Kāmeśvara is one of the several forms of शिव, as the male counterpart or spouse of कामेश्वरी, especially in the ritualistic worship of the श्रीचक्र. (See ŚRĪCAKRA.) He stands for this phenomenal world, as the presiding deity. He is also the principle governing our चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, especially our काम or desires. ‘Ka’, the first consonant of Sanskrit alphabets, represents him (k) along with his शक्ति or spouse (a). ‘Kāma’ in his name ‘Kāmeśvara’ suggests the cosmic urge to find an expression outside.

Kāmadhenu
(‘wish-yielding cow’)
------------------------------------------
Kāmadhenu, the celestial cow that fulfils all the desires, was born out of the ocean of milk when it was being churned. (See SAMUDRA MATHANA.) इन्द्र took it away.
Vasiṣṭha’s cow Nandinī is sometimes identified with कामधेनु.
According to another version, the cow सुरभि was the daughter of दक्ष. सुरभि’s offspring was रोहिणी and कामधेनु was रोहिणी’s daughter.
It is white in colour and has four feet which represent the four वेदस्. Its four udders can confer the four पुरुषार्थस्.
See PURUṢĀRTHAS.

kāmyakarma
(‘desire-motivated actions’)
------------------------------------------
A human being can never rest without performing कर्म or some sort of action or activity. Such karmas, as per the Hindu scriptures, are of four types: निषिद्धकर्म (prohibited actions); काम्यकर्म (actions motivated by desires); नित्यकर्म and naimittikakarma (obligatory actions prescribed to be performed daily and on special occasions); निष्कामकर्म (desireless actions).
Niṣiddhakarma or sinful actions like stealing, rape and murder are highly condemned and hence must be eschewed at all costs.
Kāmyakarma or desire-motivated actions are permitted to be performed to fulfil one’s desires if they cannot be got in the normal course by human efforts alone. The kāmyeṣṭis of the वेदस् and the various vratas prescribed by the पुराणस् belong to this category.
Nityakarmas are the prescribed daily duties like अग्निहोत्र, सन्ध्यावन्दन and देवपूजा (worship of family deity). Naimittikakarmas are occasional rites like śrāddhas (obsequial rites) or ड़स्तिन्ग् on certain days like ekādaśīs and so on.
Niṣkāmakarma is any good work done without selfish desires or motives, like service to others or as an offering to God or with the attitude of worship of God. This type of work purifies the मिन्द्, ultimately leading to the realisation of the Self within.
